prompt: A Harborview Hotels property reports an overnight spike in failed login attempts on staff accounts for the reservations system. The general manager wants to shut the reservations system down chain-wide immediately; the front-desk supervisor assumes it is just a glitch from a recent software update and wants to take no action. The information security manager has not yet confirmed what actually happened. What should the security manager do FIRST?

options.text: Determine what is actually known - which accounts were affected, whether any account was compromised, and whether guest payment data was accessed - before classifying the event or choosing a response.
options.rationale: An unconfirmed event isn't yet a classified incident; the response, escalation, and authority path all depend on first confirming the facts, not on either stakeholder's initial assumption.

options.text: Shut down the reservations system across the entire hotel chain, as the general manager has requested.
options.rationale: Shutting down a chain-wide system is a significant business decision with its own cost and impact - making it before confirming what actually happened, and before classifying the incident's real severity, jumps ahead of the work that decision depends on.

options.text: Take no action, accepting the front-desk supervisor's assumption that it is a routine software glitch.
options.rationale: Dismissing the report on assumption is just as risky as overreacting to it - if one of the failed-login accounts is genuinely compromised, that fact is only discoverable by checking, not by assuming it away.

options.text: Escalate the report to corporate executives immediately so they can decide how to respond.
options.rationale: Escalating before anything is confirmed gives executives nothing concrete to decide on; classification and escalation both depend on first knowing what actually happened.

explanation: Before anything else, the organization must confirm what has actually happened - an unconfirmed report is an event, not yet a classified incident. Only after confirming the facts can the incident be classified and the right response, authority, and escalation path applied. Acting on either stakeholder's assumption, in either direction, skips that necessary first step.
recognition_clue: A stem describing an incomplete or still-developing report, with stakeholders already assuming different severities, and asking what should happen FIRST, is testing whether confirmation precedes classification and action.
memory_rule: An event is not an incident until it's confirmed - don't act on assumption.

prompt: A regional grocery chain's security team discovers two separate events in the same week: a highly sophisticated exploit attempt against an unused test server holding no customer or production data, and a simpler compromise of a single cashier terminal that briefly exposed customers' payment card numbers. Which event is MOST severe from a business-impact perspective?

options.text: The cashier-terminal compromise, because it exposed actual payment card data regardless of how simple the attack itself was.
options.rationale: Severity follows business impact - the financial, legal/regulatory, and reputational exposure created by real payment card data loss - not how sophisticated or complex the attacking technique was.

options.text: The test-server exploit, because it required far greater technical skill to carry out successfully.
options.rationale: Technical sophistication describes the attacker's method, not the business consequence - a highly skilled attempt against a system holding no customer or production data creates little real impact.

options.text: Both events are equally severe, since each represents a successful compromise of a company system.
options.rationale: Treating every successful compromise as equally severe ignores the very different business impact each one actually causes - exposed payment card data is not equivalent to a probe of an empty test system.

options.text: The test-server exploit, because it will require significantly more time, effort, and specialized investigation resources to fully understand what actually happened.
options.rationale: How much investigation an event requires is an operational cost, not a measure of the business impact the event itself caused.

explanation: Severity is assessed by business impact - the financial, legal/regulatory, operational, and reputational consequences, and which specific assets were affected - not by how technically complex, skillful, or effort-intensive the underlying event was. A simple compromise that exposes real payment card data is more severe than a sophisticated attempt that exposes nothing of value.
recognition_clue: A stem contrasting a technically impressive/complex event against a simpler one, and asking which is MORE severe, is testing whether severity is assessed by business impact rather than technical drama.
memory_rule: Severity follows business impact, not technical drama.

prompt: A regional courier company wants to establish a scheme for classifying and categorizing security incidents so that response resources, authority, and escalation are applied consistently. Which approach is MOST effective?

options.text: Build a classification framework tailored to the courier company's own business context, developed with input from the stakeholders who understand that context.
options.rationale: An effective scheme reflects the organization's own operations, assets, and risk profile, built with the people who understand that context - not a scheme pulled wholesale from somewhere else.

options.text: Adopt a widely used industry-standard categorization scheme exactly as published, without modification.
options.rationale: A generic industry scheme was not built around this courier company's specific operations and assets - using it unmodified risks misclassifying what actually matters most to this business.

options.text: Assign responsibility for defining the scheme entirely to the technical incident response team.
options.rationale: The technical response team can inform the scheme, but business impact - financial, legal, operational, and reputational consequence - is what the scheme must reflect, and that requires input beyond the technical team alone.

options.text: Outsource development of the classification scheme entirely to a third-party security consultancy.
options.rationale: A third party does not carry the business context or accountability that make a classification scheme fit the organization - that understanding has to come from within, even if a consultant assists.

explanation: The most effective classification scheme is tailored to the organization's own business context and built with input from the people who understand that context - not adopted wholesale from generic industry categories, assigned to the technical response team alone, or outsourced to a third party.
recognition_clue: A stem asking what makes a classification/categorization scheme effective is testing whether the answer ties the scheme to the organization's own business context and stakeholder input.
memory_rule: A classification scheme works because it fits the organization's own business context, not because it came from a generic template.

prompt: Harborview Hotels' information security manager has confirmed and classified the compromised-account incident at one property (see D4-U3). Corporate leadership now asks for an update. What is the BEST information for the security manager to report?

options.text: The business impact of the incident and the corrective actions currently being taken.
options.rationale: Senior management needs information that supports its own decisions - business impact and what is being done about it - not a technical blow-by-blow.

options.text: A detailed, chronological log of every failed login attempt and system alert generated overnight.
options.rationale: A raw technical log does not tell leadership what it actually needs to decide - it answers a different audience's question than the one leadership is asking.

options.text: A comparison of how other hotel chains have handled similar incidents in the past.
options.rationale: Industry comparisons do not describe what happened at Harborview or what impact it is having - they are irrelevant to the decision leadership needs to make right now.

options.text: A business case for purchasing new access-control technology to prevent similar incidents in the future.
options.rationale: A future purchase decision is premature before leadership even has the current incident's impact and response - that conversation comes later, not as the incident update itself.

explanation: Senior management and executives need the business impact of an incident and the corrective actions being taken - information that supports their own decisions - not raw technical detail, unrelated comparisons, or a premature pitch for new controls.
recognition_clue: A stem asking what should be reported to senior management/executives after a classified incident is testing whether the answer matches business impact and corrective action to that audience's actual decision, not technical detail.
memory_rule: Executives need business impact and corrective action, not a raw technical log.

prompt: A reporter contacts an on-duty technical support contractor at a mid-size pharmacy chain directly, asking for comment about a security incident that was just confirmed at one of its pharmacies. The contractor has no role in media relations. What should the contractor do?

options.text: Decline to comment and direct the reporter to the organization's single authorized spokesperson.
options.rationale: Media contact should always go through one identified, pre-authorized spokesperson delivering a specifically prepared message - not whichever employee happens to be reached first.

options.text: Give the reporter a brief, factual statement about what is currently known.
options.rationale: Even a brief, well-intentioned comment from someone without that authority can conflict with the organization's prepared message or disclose something premature - media contact is not the contractor's call to make.

options.text: Refuse to comment and tell the reporter the organization will say nothing until the incident is fully resolved.
options.rationale: Refusing all comment indefinitely is not the same as routing the inquiry correctly - the organization may still need to issue a prepared statement well before full resolution.

options.text: Refer the reporter directly to law enforcement for comment.
options.rationale: Law enforcement is not the organization's spokesperson and has no role in communicating the pharmacy chain's own message - this simply redirects the problem rather than routing it correctly.

explanation: All media contact about an incident should be routed through one authorized, pre-prepared spokesperson - not handled, refused wholesale, or redirected elsewhere by whichever employee happens to be reached, since only the designated spokesperson delivers the organization's specifically prepared message.
recognition_clue: A stem describing a reporter or outside party reaching an employee directly for comment is testing whether all such contact is routed to one authorized spokesperson, not answered, refused wholesale, or redirected elsewhere.
memory_rule: Media hears from one authorized spokesperson, or not at all.
note: DOMAIN 4 U3/U4 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md, grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4B4 sub-area (the most important consideration for media interaction is a specifically drafted message from one authorized spokesperson - not refusing all comment, not referring media to authorities, and not an unplanned comment from an unauthorized employee) and the existing CANONICAL Pattern P11 (applicable_domains extended to include domain.d4 this batch) and P02, both approved for Domain 4. Original scenario, transferred to a mid-size pharmacy chain, not a reproduction of any specific source question. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

prompt: A regional telecommunications provider confirms a security incident that may involve exposure of customer data, raising possible regulatory notification obligations. Who should decide whether and how to notify regulators and affected customers?

options.text: Management, following the organization's established incident communication plan.
options.rationale: Deciding whether and how to notify external parties with legal/regulatory implications is a business decision that belongs to management, made through the organization's own communication plan - not improvised by a technical role in the moment.

options.text: The information security manager, since they identified and confirmed the incident.
options.rationale: Identifying and confirming an incident is a different responsibility than deciding how to handle its legal and regulatory consequences - that decision belongs to management, not to whoever confirmed the facts.

options.text: The incident response team, since they are actively managing the incident.
options.rationale: The response team's accountability is executing the active response, not deciding external notification obligations that carry legal and regulatory consequences for the organization.

options.text: The third-party managed-service provider whose systems were involved, since it is closest to the technical details of what happened.
options.rationale: A third party's involvement in the technical details does not transfer the organization's own accountability for deciding external notification - that decision, and its consequences, remain the organization's to make.

explanation: Deciding whether and how to notify regulators, customers, or other external parties after an incident with legal implications is a business decision that belongs to management, made through the organization's own communication plan - not a call the information security manager, the incident response team, or an involved third party can make on the organization's behalf.
recognition_clue: A stem asking who decides whether/how to notify regulators or customers after a confirmed incident with legal implications is testing whether that authority is correctly placed with management, not a technical role or an involved third party.
memory_rule: External notification is a management decision, following the communication plan - a third party's involvement never transfers that accountability away.
note: DOMAIN 4 U3/U4 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md, grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4B4 sub-area (communication regarding security events with legal implications is explicitly a business decision belonging to management, not the information security manager contacting external authorities directly) and the existing CANONICAL Pattern P11 (applicable_domains extended to include domain.d4 this batch) and P02 (Authority Follows Accountability), both approved for Domain 4. Original scenario, transferred to a regional telecommunications provider, not a reproduction of any specific source question. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

prompt: Harborview Hotels has classified and escalated the compromised-account incident at one property (see D4-U3/D4-U4). The property's general manager wants the entire reservations system shut down chain-wide to be safe. The incident response team has confirmed the compromise is limited to this property's own reservation server. What is the BEST containment approach?

options.text: Isolate the affected property's reservation server from the network, leaving the reservations system at Harborview's other properties running normally.
options.rationale: Containment should limit further harm at the scope the incident actually affects - isolating the specific affected component protects the organization without disrupting business operations that were never at risk.

options.text: Shut down the reservations system chain-wide, as the general manager requested, to be certain nothing else is affected.
options.rationale: A chain-wide shutdown disrupts every property's ability to take reservations even though only one property's server was actually affected - containment should match the incident's actual scope, not the most cautious-sounding option.

options.text: Wait until the incident response team has determined the root cause before taking any containment action.
options.rationale: Containment is the priority once an incident is confirmed - waiting for root-cause analysis, which is part of eradication, delays limiting the harm that is happening right now.

options.text: Immediately restore the affected server from the most recent backup so reservations can resume as quickly as possible.
options.rationale: Restoring from backup before the affected server has been properly contained and evidence preserved risks reintroducing whatever caused the compromise, and can destroy evidence needed to understand what happened.

explanation: Containment should limit further harm at the scope the incident actually affects - not the broadest possible shutdown, not a delay for root-cause analysis (which belongs to eradication), and not an immediate restore that risks reinfection and destroys evidence.
recognition_clue: A stem offering a broad, indiscriminate shutdown alongside a narrower, scope-appropriate isolation option is testing whether containment is matched to the incident's actual impact, not the most cautious-sounding action.
memory_rule: Contain at the scope the incident actually affects - not the broadest possible shutdown.
note: DOMAIN 4 U5/U6 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md, grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4B3 (Incident Containment Methods) sub-area (isolating the affected network segment/system, not an indiscriminate broad shutdown, is repeatedly preferred; root-cause analysis is explicitly identified as part of eradication, which follows containment; restoring from backup before containment risks reinfection and destroys evidence) and the existing CANONICAL Pattern P01 (Business Alignment) and P04 (No Lifecycle Jumping), both already approved for Domain 4. Original scenario, not a reproduction or paraphrase of any specific source question. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

prompt: A regional manufacturing company confirms that ransomware has encrypted files on several production-line control workstations. What should the incident response team do FIRST?

options.text: Remove the affected workstations from the network to stop the ransomware from spreading further.
options.rationale: Once an incident is confirmed, containment - limiting further spread - is the immediate priority, ahead of restoration, notification, or further log review.

options.text: Restore the affected workstations from the most recent backup so production can resume.
options.rationale: Restoring before containing risks reinfecting the restored systems if the backup itself was already compromised, and can destroy evidence needed to understand how the ransomware spread.

options.text: Notify the affected workstations' system owners before taking any technical action.
options.rationale: Notification matters, but spending time notifying owners first allows the ransomware to keep spreading to additional systems while nothing is contained.

options.text: Review event logs across the network to identify every system that may be infected before acting.
options.rationale: A full log review takes time the business can't afford while ransomware continues spreading uncontained - containing the systems already identified comes first.

explanation: Once ransomware is confirmed, the immediate priority is containment - removing the affected systems from the network to stop further spread - ahead of restoration (which risks reinfection and destroys evidence), notification, or a comprehensive log review.
recognition_clue: A stem describing active, spreading malware and asking what should happen FIRST is testing whether containment is recognized as the immediate priority, ahead of recovery, notification, or a full investigation.
memory_rule: Containment limits harm; it doesn't mean the threat is gone, systems are restored, or the incident is over.
note: DOMAIN 4 U5/U6 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md, grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4B3 sub-area (ransomware scenario: removing affected systems from the network is identified as the FIRST step/containment phase after confirmation; restoring from backup first risks reinfection and 'would destroy evidence needed to investigate the incident'; reviewing logs before containing allows continued uncontained spread) and the existing CANONICAL Pattern P01 and P04, both already approved for Domain 4. Original scenario, transferred to a regional manufacturing company, not a reproduction of any specific source question. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

prompt: A national logistics company's security team detects an active data exfiltration in progress - a compromised server is actively sending data to an external destination. What should the team do FIRST?

options.text: Block outbound traffic from the compromised server to the external destination.
options.rationale: The immediate priority is stopping the ongoing loss of data - blocking the outbound connection limits the harm right now without requiring the system to be powered off.

options.text: Power off the compromised server to stop the exfiltration immediately.
options.rationale: Powering off the server causes a state change that can destroy volatile evidence, such as active connections and memory contents, needed to understand how the exfiltration occurred - without being the only way to stop it.

options.text: Determine the root cause of how the server was compromised before taking any action.
options.rationale: Determining the root cause is part of eradication, which follows containment - waiting for it first allows the exfiltration to continue.

options.text: Inform the server's system owner and wait for their direction before acting.
options.rationale: The incident response team has the responsibility to take immediate containment action against active harm; the system owner should be informed, but that does not need to precede stopping the ongoing exfiltration.

explanation: Against active, ongoing data exfiltration, the immediate priority is stopping the loss of data - blocking the outbound connection - rather than powering off the system (which destroys volatile evidence), waiting to determine root cause (which follows containment), or waiting for the system owner's direction before acting.
recognition_clue: A stem describing active data exfiltration and offering an immediate power-off alongside a more targeted blocking action is testing whether the learner recognizes that a full power-off can destroy the volatile evidence a targeted block does not.
memory_rule: A fast technical fix that destroys evidence isn't actually faster once that evidence is needed later.
note: DOMAIN 4 U5/U6 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md, grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4B3 sub-area (active exfiltration scenario, source verbatim: 'the priority... would be to limit the damage by blocking outgoing traffic to the attacker's servers'; turning the system off 'will result in a state change, which may result in the loss of forensic evidence'; determining the cause 'would not be the first action to take'; informing the system owner 'is not the first thing... should focus on') and the existing CANONICAL Pattern P01 and P04, both already approved for Domain 4. Original scenario, transferred to a national logistics company, not a reproduction of any specific source question. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

prompt: Harborview's IT team, eager to restore reservations service at the affected property, wants to wipe and reimage the isolated server's original hard drive immediately. What should the security manager direct FIRST?

options.text: Create a verified copy of the original hard drive and preserve the original untouched before any rebuild proceeds.
options.rationale: Rebuilding from the original destroys evidence the organization may later need for legal, regulatory, or disciplinary purposes - preserving a verified copy keeps that evidence intact while restoration proceeds from the copy.

options.text: Proceed with wiping and reimaging the original hard drive immediately, since restoring service is the priority now that the server is contained.
options.rationale: Containment limits harm, but it doesn't mean evidence no longer matters - wiping the original before it's preserved destroys exactly what a later investigation might need.

options.text: Perform the forensic analysis directly on the original hard drive to save time before restoring service.
options.rationale: Working from the original risks contaminating the only original evidence - forensic analysis should be performed on a verified copy instead.

options.text: Delay any restoration until law enforcement has completed its own investigation of the server.
options.rationale: Whether and when law enforcement is involved is a decision senior management makes based on the circumstances - assuming law enforcement must finish first, or must be involved at all, is not something the security manager should presume unilaterally.

explanation: Evidence has to be preserved before a system is rebuilt or restored, not after - a verified copy of the original media keeps the evidence intact for any later legal, regulatory, or disciplinary need, while restoration proceeds from that copy rather than the original.
recognition_clue: A stem describing pressure to restore, rebuild, or reimage a system quickly, offered before evidence has been preserved, is testing whether the learner recognizes evidence preservation as the necessary first step.
memory_rule: Investigate from a copy, not the original.
note: DOMAIN 4 U5/U6 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md, grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4B2 (Incident Investigation and Evaluation) sub-area (forensic analysis 'must be performed only on a copy of the original media so that the evidence is uncontaminated'; a write blocker is used 'to maintain the integrity of the original storage media'; rebuilding a compromised system risks losing evidence needed to understand how the incident occurred) and the existing CANONICAL Pattern P04 (No Lifecycle Jumping) and P02 (Authority Follows Accountability), both already approved for Domain 4. Continues Harborview Hotels directly from D4-U5's contained incident. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

prompt: A regional healthcare provider's incident response team has preserved evidence from a compromised server that may support later legal action. What is the PRIMARY reason to maintain a documented chain of custody for that evidence?

options.text: To keep the evidence admissible and credible by tracing who had control of it throughout the investigation.
options.rationale: Chain of custody exists to preserve the integrity of evidence so it remains valid and admissible for legal or regulatory proceedings - that is its primary purpose.

options.text: To keep the enterprise's asset inventory updated with the affected system's current custodian.
options.rationale: Chain of custody is not related to asset inventory or ownership tracking - it documents control of evidence, not asset custodianship.

options.text: To identify which individual compromised the system.
options.rationale: Identifying who compromised the system is a possible outcome of forensic analysis, not the reason chain of custody itself is maintained.

options.text: To ensure the evidence is stored exclusively on read-only media.
options.rationale: Read-only storage can help prevent tampering, but chain of custody itself is the documented record of control - not a specific storage requirement.

explanation: Chain of custody is a documented, unbroken record of who controlled a piece of evidence and when. Its primary purpose is to keep that evidence admissible and credible for legal, regulatory, or disciplinary proceedings - not to track asset ownership, identify an attacker, or dictate a specific storage medium.
recognition_clue: A stem asking why chain of custody matters, or what its primary purpose is, is testing whether the learner ties it to evidence admissibility/credibility rather than an unrelated concern.
memory_rule: A broken chain of custody is a bigger risk than physical damage to the evidence - it undermines whether the evidence can be trusted at all.
note: DOMAIN 4 U5/U6 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md, grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4B2 sub-area, directly source-confirmed verbatim ('the PRIMARY reason to ensure chain of custody is... the forensic evidence is valid and admissible in a court of law'; 'chain of custody is not related to the asset custodian or to updating the asset inventory'; a broken chain of custody was identified as the MOST significant concern in a mishandled-evidence scenario, ahead of physical damage to the drives themselves) and the existing CANONICAL Pattern P02 and P04, both already approved for Domain 4. Original scenario, transferred to a regional healthcare provider, not a reproduction of any specific source question. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

prompt: A national retail chain confirms that a compromised point-of-sale system may support criminal charges against an identified suspect. Store operations is pressing to restore the system immediately to resume sales. What should be the incident response team's MOST important priority?

options.text: Preventing contamination of the evidence, since preserving it can outweigh the pressure to restore service quickly when criminal charges may follow.
options.rationale: When an incident may lead to criminal charges, preserving uncontaminated evidence takes on added importance - restoring service too quickly, before evidence is preserved, can destroy what a later prosecution would need.

options.text: Restoring the system immediately, since limiting business disruption always comes first.
options.rationale: Business disruption matters, but it does not always come first - when criminal charges may follow, contaminating the evidence needed to support that case is a cost that outweighs a faster restoration.

options.text: Waiting for law enforcement to arrive on-site before taking any action to preserve evidence.
options.rationale: Evidence preservation doesn't wait for law enforcement to arrive - the response team can and should preserve evidence themselves in the meantime.

options.text: Letting the incident response team decide independently whether to notify law enforcement, since they identified the incident.
options.rationale: Deciding whether to notify law enforcement is senior management's decision, not the incident response team's to make on its own, even though the team identified the incident.

explanation: When an incident may lead to criminal charges, preventing contamination of evidence takes on added weight - it can outweigh the pressure to restore service quickly, since a faster restoration that destroys evidence undermines the very case the organization may need to support. This is a scoped refinement of containment-first sequencing, not a rule that evidence always outranks every other priority.
recognition_clue: A stem describing restoration pressure against a backdrop of possible criminal charges is testing whether the learner recognizes evidence preservation as taking on elevated priority in that specific context, and correctly places law-enforcement-notification authority with senior management.
memory_rule: Restoring too quickly can destroy the evidence a later decision needs - in situations that may lead to criminal charges, preserving evidence can outweigh the pressure to restore fast.
note: DOMAIN 4 U5/U6 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md, grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4B1/4B2 sub-areas, directly source-confirmed verbatim ('preventing contamination of evidence takes priority over containment in situations where criminal charges may be filed'; 'in many enterprises, the decision to notify law enforcement is made by senior management') and the existing CANONICAL Pattern P02 and P04, both already approved for Domain 4. This variant's evidence-outranks-speed reasoning is deliberately scoped to the criminal-charges context the source itself uses, not generalized into an absolute rule - see concept.d4.evidence-investigation's note for the full source-nuance discussion. Original scenario, transferred to a national retail chain, not a reproduction of any specific source question. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

prompt: With the original hard drive preserved (see D4-U6), Harborview's IT team wants to restore reservations service quickly by reinstalling the system from last week's backup. The security manager instead directs the team to rebuild the server from the original, clean installation media. What is the BEST reason for this decision?

options.text: The compromised account had privileged access, and a backup taken after the compromise could carry the same exposure forward - rebuilding from known-clean original media is what actually confirms the cause is gone.
options.rationale: When a compromise involves privileged access, a backup taken afterward cannot be trusted to be clean - only a rebuild from known-clean original media reliably confirms the cause has actually been removed.

options.text: Restoring from backup takes longer than rebuilding from original media, so rebuilding gets reservations service back online faster.
options.rationale: Rebuilding from original media is not chosen for speed - it is generally the slower option - but for the assurance that the cause has genuinely been removed, which a possibly-compromised backup cannot provide.

options.text: The affected account has already been isolated, so rebuilding from either source is equally safe at this point.
options.rationale: Isolating the account was containment, not eradication - it stopped further spread but did not remove the cause, so the backup itself can still carry the same exposure forward.

options.text: Law enforcement must approve the rebuild method before the team proceeds.
options.rationale: Rebuilding from clean media is a technical eradication decision, not one that requires law-enforcement approval - no source-supported rule makes external approval a precondition here.

explanation: When a compromise involves privileged or administrative access, a backup taken after the compromise cannot be trusted to be clean - it can carry the same exposure forward. Rebuilding from known-clean, original installation media is what actually confirms the cause has been removed, which is what eradication requires.
recognition_clue: A stem describing a privileged-account compromise and offering a recent backup as the fast restoration option is testing whether the learner recognizes that backup could carry the same exposure forward - rebuilding from known-clean original media is the reliable answer.
memory_rule: After a privileged-access compromise, rebuild from clean original media - a backup taken afterward can't be fully trusted.
note: DOMAIN 4 U7/U8 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md, grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4B5 (Incident Eradication and Recovery) sub-area (when a superuser/privileged account is compromised, 'rebuilding the system from the original installation medium is the only way to ensure all security vulnerabilities and potential stealth malicious programs have been destroyed' - explicitly not a verified backup, since 'the verified backup may have been compromised by the super-user at a different time') and the existing CANONICAL Pattern P04 (No Lifecycle Jumping) and P05 (No Lifecycle Reversal), both already approved for Domain 4. Continues Harborview Hotels directly from D4-U6's preserved evidence. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

prompt: A regional airline's IT team restores its booking system within the recovery time objective and reports the incident resolved. Passengers, however, still cannot complete payment for new bookings. What is the MOST accurate conclusion for the security manager to reach?

options.text: Recovery is not actually complete - meeting the recovery time objective does not guarantee the business function has been fully, verifiably restored.
options.rationale: A recovery time objective is a target, sometimes a minimum acceptable operating level - it does not by itself prove recovery is complete. Only verifying the business's own processes are genuinely working end to end, including payment, confirms that.

options.text: The incident is resolved, since the recovery time objective was the stated target and it was met.
options.rationale: Meeting a stated recovery time objective is not the same as recovery being complete - the booking system is back online, but the payment function it depends on is not yet working.

options.text: The team should begin the post-incident review now that recovery is finished.
options.rationale: Recovery is not actually finished while a core business function still isn't working - moving to post-incident review skips ahead of the verification recovery still requires.

options.text: This is now an eradication problem, since the payment issue suggests the original cause was never fully removed.
options.rationale: An unverified business function points to an incomplete recovery, not necessarily a failure of eradication - the two are distinct concerns, and nothing in the scenario suggests the original cause is still present.

explanation: A recovery time objective is a target, not proof of full recovery - it can represent a minimum acceptable operating level well short of normal operations. Only verifying that the organization's own business processes are genuinely working end to end confirms recovery is actually complete.
recognition_clue: A stem stating a recovery time objective has been met, while a business function is still visibly not working, is testing whether the learner treats RTO as a target rather than proof of complete recovery.
memory_rule: Meeting the recovery time objective isn't the same as recovery being complete - verify the business itself is actually working again.
note: DOMAIN 4 U7/U8 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md, grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4B5 sub-area ('RTO is an objective, and full restoration may or may not coincide with the RTO... RTO can be the minimum acceptable operational level, far short of normal operations'; 'until end-to-end transaction flow is established, recovery is not complete... whether the RTO has been met is less important than achieving full recovery') and the existing CANONICAL Pattern P04 and P05, both already approved for Domain 4. Original scenario, transferred to a regional airline, not a reproduction of any specific source question. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

prompt: A national manufacturing company's incident response team reports: "The malicious account has been isolated, and we've confirmed the malware has been completely removed from all affected systems. Production systems have not yet been reconnected." What should happen NEXT?

options.text: Begin restoring and reconnecting production systems, verifying normal operation as recovery proceeds.
options.rationale: Containment and eradication have both already been confirmed complete - the next step is recovery: restoring and verifying the affected systems, not repeating a step already finished or declaring the incident over before it is.

options.text: Continue containment efforts, since the incident isn't fully resolved yet.
options.rationale: Containment has already been completed - the scenario states the malicious account was isolated. Continuing containment retreats to a stage that has already passed rather than addressing what comes next.

options.text: Begin eradication procedures to remove the malware from the affected systems.
options.rationale: The malware has already been confirmed completely removed - eradication is complete. Repeating it retreats to a stage that has already passed rather than moving to recovery.

options.text: Declare the incident closed immediately, since the malicious account has been isolated and the malware removed.
options.rationale: Recovery - restoring and verifying the production systems - has not yet happened. Declaring the incident closed before systems are reconnected and verified skips ahead of what containment and eradication being complete actually requires next.

explanation: The correct response always matches what the scenario has already established. Containment and eradication are both confirmed complete here, so the next step is recovery - restoring and verifying the affected systems - not repeating a completed stage and not declaring the incident closed before recovery has actually happened.
recognition_clue: A stem stating that containment and eradication are both already complete, and asking what happens NEXT, is testing whether the learner correctly identifies recovery rather than retreating to an already-finished stage or jumping to closure.
memory_rule: Stopping the damage isn't removing the cause, and removing the cause isn't safely restoring the business - each is a separate, necessary step.
note: DOMAIN 4 U7/U8 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md, grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4B5 sub-area (eradication 'requires determining and eliminating the root cause,' explicitly distinguished from containment and from recovery, which is 'accomplished after eradication and during recovery phase') and the existing CANONICAL Pattern P04 (No Lifecycle Jumping) and P05 (No Lifecycle Reversal), both already approved for Domain 4 - this question is the first full-strength reuse of P05 in Domain 4 production content. Original scenario, transferred to a national manufacturing company, not a reproduction of any specific source question. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

prompt: While Harborview's reservation server is being rebuilt (see D4-U7), the property's general manager reports that front-desk staff are checking guests in manually using a paper-based process, since the reservation system remains unavailable. The regional operations director asks which plan governs this manual check-in process. What is the correct answer?

options.text: The business continuity plan - it keeps the critical guest check-in process running while the underlying technology is still being restored, distinct from the disaster recovery plan restoring the server itself.
options.rationale: Business continuity keeps critical business processes running when normal operations are disrupted - the manual check-in workaround is exactly that, and it is a distinct concern from the technical work of restoring the interrupted system.

options.text: The incident response plan, since the security incident is still active.
options.rationale: Incident response manages the security incident itself - it does not govern a business-process workaround for keeping guest check-in running while the incident is being handled.

options.text: The disaster recovery plan, since it covers all recovery-related activity during an incident.
options.rationale: Disaster recovery restores specific interrupted technology, systems, or data - it does not govern a manual business-process workaround, which is a business continuity concern instead.

options.text: No formal plan governs this - the front-desk staff improvised a reasonable workaround.
options.rationale: A business continuity plan exists precisely to have a defined process ready for exactly this situation - treating it as an improvised, unplanned response misses that this is what business continuity planning is for.

explanation: Business continuity keeps critical business processes running - the actual work of the organization, not just its technology - when normal operations are disrupted. The manual check-in workaround is business continuity in action, distinct from disaster recovery's job of restoring the interrupted server itself.
recognition_clue: A stem describing a manual or workaround process keeping a business function running while its usual system is down is testing whether the learner recognizes that as business continuity, not a sign that no plan applies, and distinct from the technology restoration itself.
memory_rule: Business continuity keeps the business's own processes running - it isn't just another name for restoring IT.
note: DOMAIN 4 U7/U8 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md, grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4A3/4A4 sub-areas ('MOST closely associated with a business continuity program' is 'developing recovery time objectives for critical functions,' explicitly rejecting technical-recovery-plan/network-redundancy/equipment-configuration options as all 'associated with infrastructure disaster recovery' instead; 'the disaster recovery plan (DRP) focuses on restoring IT systems and data. This is not necessarily covered when testing the business continuity plan (BCP)') and the existing CANONICAL Pattern P01 (Business Alignment), already approved for Domain 4. Continues Harborview Hotels directly from D4-U7's recovery-in-progress incident. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

prompt: A mid-size hospital system's disaster recovery team is designing its backup strategy for the patient records database. Leadership states that losing more than 15 minutes of recently entered data would be unacceptable, but the system can remain offline for up to 4 hours without material harm. Which recovery objective is the PRIMARY driver of how frequently the database must be backed up?

options.text: The recovery point objective (RPO) - the maximum tolerable data loss, not the allowable downtime, is what determines backup frequency.
options.rationale: Backup frequency exists to limit how much data could be lost, which is exactly what the recovery point objective defines - the stated 15-minute data-loss tolerance directly sets how often backups must run.

options.text: The recovery time objective (RTO) - it describes the allowable downtime, which directly drives how often the database must be backed up.
options.rationale: RTO describes allowable downtime, not tolerable data loss - it does not drive backup frequency, which depends on how much data the organization can afford to lose, not how long it can be offline.

options.text: The maximum tolerable outage (MTO) - it describes the outer limit before impact becomes unacceptable, which drives how often backups must run.
options.rationale: MTO describes the absolute outer limit the organization can operate in alternate mode - it is a time-based ceiling, not the data-loss tolerance that determines backup frequency.

options.text: The service delivery objective (SDO) - it describes the level of service during alternate operation, which drives how often backups must run.
options.rationale: SDO describes the level of service maintained during alternate operation, not tolerable data loss - it does not determine how frequently the database must be backed up.

explanation: The recovery point objective is the maximum tolerable data loss, measured in time - it is what directly determines backup frequency, not the recovery time objective (allowable downtime), the maximum tolerable outage (the outer time limit), or the service delivery objective (the alternate-mode service level).
recognition_clue: A stem stating a specific tolerable-data-loss figure alongside a separate tolerable-downtime figure, and asking what drives backup frequency, is testing whether the learner correctly matches data loss to RPO rather than confusing it with RTO, MTO, or SDO.
memory_rule: RTO is downtime, RPO is data loss, SDO is the service level during alternate operation - three separate business-defined commitments, not interchangeable.

prompt: A national telecommunications provider's disaster recovery team restores its customer-service call center at a warm site, but it can currently handle only half its normal call volume. The team reports this as a successful recovery milestone. Which recovery objective MOST accurately describes what has actually been met?

options.text: The service delivery objective (SDO) - the agreed level of service during alternate operation, not a specific time target or data-loss limit.
options.rationale: The service delivery objective is the level of service to be reached during alternate processing until normal operation is restored - a warm site operating at half capacity is describing exactly that, not a time target or a data-loss limit.

options.text: The recovery time objective (RTO), since the call center is back online within the target window.
options.rationale: RTO describes how long a function can be down, not the level of service once it is back - operating at half capacity describes a service level, which RTO does not measure.

options.text: The recovery point objective (RPO), since no customer data appears to have been lost.
options.rationale: RPO describes tolerable data loss, which is unrelated to call-handling capacity - nothing in the scenario concerns data loss at all.

options.text: Full recovery has been achieved, since the call center is operational again.
options.rationale: Operating at half capacity is a defined interim service level, not full or normal recovery - the call center is functioning, but not yet at its normal operating level.

explanation: The service delivery objective is the level of service maintained during alternate operation until normal conditions are restored. A warm site running at half capacity is describing that service level directly - it is not a time target (RTO), a data-loss limit (RPO), or proof that full, normal recovery has been reached.
recognition_clue: A stem describing a system restored to a specific, partial capacity level - not a time elapsed or data lost - is testing whether the learner correctly matches that fact to SDO rather than RTO or RPO.
memory_rule: RTO is downtime, RPO is data loss, SDO is the service level during alternate operation - three separate business-defined commitments, not interchangeable.

prompt: Harborview's post-incident review identifies the overnight monitoring gap as the root cause that allowed the compromise to go undetected for hours, and recommends implementing real-time, 24/7 alerting on privileged-account activity. Once the recommendation is written up, Harborview's executive team schedules a formal review of the incident. What is the PRIMARY reason for that executive review?

options.text: To confirm that the recommended corrective action - real-time monitoring - has actually been implemented, not merely recommended in the report.
options.rationale: Senior management's review of an incident exists primarily to confirm that adequate corrective actions were actually put in place - a recommendation on paper is not the same as a completed improvement.

options.text: To evaluate how well the security team performed while responding to the incident.
options.rationale: Management does not review an incident to evaluate or fault the response team's own performance - that turns the review into fault-finding rather than confirming improvement.

options.text: To demonstrate to the board that management takes information security seriously.
options.rationale: The review is not conducted merely to demonstrate management commitment - its purpose is verifying that a specific, concrete corrective action was actually implemented.

options.text: To determine which employee should be held responsible for the account compromise.
options.rationale: Assigning individual responsibility for the compromise is blame-finding, not the review's purpose - the review exists to confirm the process itself has been improved.

explanation: Senior management's review of a completed incident exists primarily to confirm that adequate corrective actions were actually implemented - not to evaluate the response team's performance, demonstrate commitment, or assign individual blame. A recommendation written up in a report is not yet a completed improvement.
recognition_clue: A stem describing an executive or senior-management review of a completed incident, with fault-finding or symbolic options offered as distractors, is testing whether the learner recognizes the review's purpose is confirming corrective action, not finding fault.
memory_rule: Senior management reviews an incident to confirm corrective actions were implemented, not to find fault.

prompt: A regional university's incident response team eradicated a compromised account and restored affected systems, but was never able to conclusively determine how the account was originally compromised. What should the post-incident review do regarding this open question NEXT?

options.text: Complete the root-cause analysis, since understanding how the compromise occurred is necessary to prevent it from recurring.
options.rationale: Root-cause analysis is normally first examined during eradication, but when it is not fully resolved there, post-incident review is where that understanding should be completed - not skipped.

options.text: Treat the incident as closed, since eradication and recovery are both already complete.
options.rationale: An incident is not genuinely closed, from a management-learning standpoint, until the root cause is understood and corrective action is confirmed - eradication and recovery alone don't establish that.

options.text: Begin a fresh vulnerability assessment instead, since eradication is already finished.
options.rationale: A vulnerability assessment identifies existing weaknesses generally - it does not determine how this specific compromise actually occurred, which is what a root-cause analysis is for.

options.text: Assign responsibility for the unresolved compromise to the IT operations team.
options.rationale: Assigning responsibility before the cause is even understood is blame ahead of understanding - the review's purpose is completing the analysis, not finding someone to hold accountable for it.

explanation: Root-cause analysis is normally first examined during eradication; when it is not fully resolved by that point, post-incident review is the appropriate place to complete it - not to treat the incident as closed, substitute a different technique, or assign blame before the cause is understood.
recognition_clue: A stem describing eradication and recovery as complete but the root cause never fully determined is testing whether the learner recognizes post-incident review as where that unfinished analysis should be completed, not skipped or reassigned to blame.
memory_rule: An incident isn't closed, from a management-learning standpoint, until what happened becomes confirmed corrective action.

prompt: A national financial services firm's post-incident review team is deciding what the review should actually produce. What should be the PRIMARY goal of the review?

options.text: Derive specific ways to improve the incident response process going forward.
options.rationale: The primary goal of a post-incident review is deriving concrete ways the incident response process can be improved - everything else the review might touch is secondary to that.

options.text: Produce a detailed report documenting every step taken during the incident.
options.rationale: The incident should already have been documented during the response itself - the review relies on that documentation to learn from it, rather than existing to produce it.

options.text: Identify which staff members failed to follow procedure so appropriate action can be taken.
options.rationale: The review should not focus on finding and addressing individuals who did not take appropriate action - that is fault-finding, not the review's purpose.

options.text: Gather additional evidence in case legal action becomes necessary.
options.rationale: Evidence relevant to potential legal action should already have been secured during the earlier investigation - gathering it is not the post-incident review's own goal.

explanation: The primary goal of a post-incident review is deriving concrete ways to improve the incident response process - not producing documentation (which should already exist from the response itself), finding fault with individuals, or gathering legal evidence (which belongs to the earlier investigation).
recognition_clue: A stem asking for the PRIMARY or MOST important goal of a post-incident review, with documentation, blame, or evidence-gathering offered as distractors, is testing whether the learner identifies process improvement as the actual goal.
memory_rule: Recovery restores operations - post-incident review improves the organization.
note: DOMAIN 4 U9/U10 AUTHORING BATCH CANDIDATE — authored by Claude Code per the approved docs/learning/DOMAIN-4-CURRICULUM-ARCHITECTURE.md, grounded in the supplied Domain 4 source material's 4B6 sub-area ('the PRIMARY goal of a post-incident review is to... derive ways to improve the response process,' explicitly rejecting gathering legal evidence, identifying individuals who failed to act, and preparing a report as the primary goal in the same source item) and the existing CANONICAL Pattern P15 and P02, both already approved for Domain 4. Original scenario, transferred to a national financial services firm, not a reproduction of any specific source question. Not yet human-reviewed or promoted.

prompt: Eight months after the reservation-server incident, another Harborview property reports a fresh wave of failed logins on a privileged account overnight. The real-time monitoring implemented after the post-incident review (see D4-U9) catches it immediately and pages the on-call security analyst before dawn. Early triage shows the account was not actually compromised - a legitimate employee had mistyped their password repeatedly after a system update. Separately, the property's general manager, still worried after last year's incident, has already told a local reporter that Harborview is "handling another attempted breach." What should the security manager treat as MOST important right now?

options.text: Correcting the general manager's unauthorized comment through Harborview's single authorized spokesperson, while confirming - based on the triage findings - that this specific event does not meet the bar for treating it as a confirmed incident.
options.rationale: The monitoring worked exactly as intended, and triage already shows this event is not a confirmed incident - what remains genuinely open is the unauthorized media comment, which needs correcting through the single authorized spokesperson regardless of how the login activity resolves.

options.text: Escalating immediately to corporate leadership as a confirmed repeat security incident, matching the severity of last year's event.
options.rationale: Triage has already shown the account was not actually compromised - treating an unconfirmed, likely-false-positive event as a confirmed incident of equal severity ignores what the facts actually establish.

options.text: Letting the general manager continue speaking with the reporter, since they already have an established relationship with that outlet.
options.rationale: An existing media relationship doesn't authorize the general manager to speak on Harborview's behalf about a security matter - that authority belongs to the single designated spokesperson.

options.text: Documenting in detail that the new monitoring control successfully triggered exactly as designed, then treating the entire overnight matter as fully closed and resolved on that basis alone, since the control itself clearly worked as intended this time.
options.rationale: The monitoring control working correctly is genuinely good news, but it doesn't resolve the separate, still-open problem of the general manager's unauthorized comment to the media.

explanation: This situation raises more than one concern at once: whether the login activity is a genuine incident, and whether the general manager's unauthorized media comment needs correcting. Triage already answers the first question - the monitoring worked and the account was not compromised - so what remains genuinely open, and MOST important right now, is routing the media response through the single authorized spokesperson.
recognition_clue: A stem describing more than one thing happening at once - a technical event already resolving one way, and a separate authority or communication problem still open - is testing whether the learner identifies what genuinely still needs action, not just the most technically interesting thread.
memory_rule: A corrective action working as intended doesn't mean every other concern in the same situation is resolved.

prompt: A mid-size hospital system's IT team detects unusual activity on a non-critical research-data server, confirmed to hold no patient-care or billing data. A department head wants the entire hospital network taken offline "to be safe." Separately, a junior communications staffer wants to publicly notify patients immediately "in case something is wrong." What should the security manager do?

options.text: Contain the activity at the scope it actually affects - the research-data server, not the entire network - and direct that no public notification occurs until management, following the organization's own communication plan, determines what is actually confirmed and required.
options.rationale: Containment should match the incident's actual, confirmed impact rather than the broadest possible action, and external notification is a management decision under the organization's own communication plan - not a call the communications staff can make unilaterally, especially before the facts are confirmed.

options.text: Take the entire hospital network offline as requested, since patient safety is always the highest priority.
options.rationale: Patient-care systems are confirmed unaffected here - an indiscriminate, network-wide shutdown disrupts operations that were never actually at risk, without a demonstrated security benefit.

options.text: Authorize the communications staffer to notify patients immediately, since transparency reduces reputational risk.
options.rationale: Notifying patients is a business/legal decision belonging to management under the organization's communication plan, not a call a communications staffer can make unilaterally - especially before the facts are confirmed.

options.text: Delay containment until forensic evidence has been fully imaged from the research-data server.
options.rationale: Containment should not wait for formal evidence imaging to complete - evidence must be protected during containment, not used as a reason to delay a proportionate containment action.

explanation: The correct response integrates two Domain 4 reasoning targets at once: containment scoped to actual, confirmed business impact rather than indiscriminate caution, and external notification routed through management's own authority and communication plan rather than decided unilaterally by whichever staff member raises it.
recognition_clue: A stem offering both an overbroad technical response and an unauthorized external-communication shortcut is testing whether the learner can integrate proportionate containment with correct notification authority at the same time.
memory_rule: Contain at the scope the incident actually affects - not the broadest possible shutdown - and route external communication through management's own authority.

prompt: A regional airline's disaster recovery team restores its booking system after eradicating a compromised account, meeting the stated recovery time objective. Meanwhile, gate agents at several airports continue checking in passengers manually, since the booking system's outage triggered the airline's business continuity plan. Corporate leadership wants to declare the entire event closed now that the system is back online. What is the BEST recommendation for the security manager to make?

options.text: Confirm the booking system is genuinely restored end to end - not just within the recovery time objective - and complete a post-incident review to identify what allowed the compromise, before declaring the incident closed.
options.rationale: Meeting a recovery time objective doesn't by itself prove recovery is complete, and an incident isn't genuinely closed, from a management-learning standpoint, until the root cause is understood and corrective action is confirmed - both still need to happen here.

options.text: Declare the incident closed, since the recovery time objective was met and gate agents can now use the booking system again.
options.rationale: Meeting the recovery time objective is not the same as recovery being complete, and it doesn't address whether the root cause was ever understood or corrective action confirmed.

options.text: Treat the matter as fully resolved because the manual check-in process kept the airline operating throughout the outage.
options.rationale: Business continuity working as intended is a genuine success, but it is a different concern from whether the underlying incident has actually been investigated and closed out.

options.text: Escalate to the board immediately as an unresolved crisis, since the incident is not technically closed yet.
options.rationale: Recovery and business continuity both worked as intended here - what remains is completing the post-incident review, not escalating this as an ongoing crisis.

explanation: This scenario integrates two Domain 4 reasoning targets: recovery is not verified simply because a recovery time objective was met, and business continuity working successfully is a separate concern from whether the incident's root cause has actually been understood and closed out through post-incident review.
recognition_clue: A stem where a recovery metric has been met and a continuity plan has worked, but leadership wants to declare the matter closed anyway, is testing whether the learner recognizes that neither fact alone proves the incident is genuinely finished.
memory_rule: An incident isn't closed, from a management-learning standpoint, until what happened becomes confirmed corrective action.
